summary: A Network Host Status report covering July 17 to July 28, 1972. The new IMP software was released on Tuesday, July 18.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

questions: what do the host status codes mean
subtitle: BBN's status report on ARPANET hosts for July 17 to July 28, 1972, including the new IMP software release.

tldr.problem: Users of the early network needed to know which hosts were working and available as servers.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts from its Terminal IMP on selected dates and recorded each result as a one-letter code, next to a table of each host's status or prediction.
tldr.outcome: The report notes that new IMP software was released on Tuesday, July 18. It updates RFC 367 and was itself updated by RFC 376.

today: RFC 370 is a historical host status report. It updates RFC 367 and is updated by RFC 376. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: What the Report Covers
sections.content:
This RFC reports on the status of most network hosts from July 17 to July 28 (1972, per the RFC's date). On Tuesday, July 18, the new IMP software was released.

Several hosts were excluded from the daily testing because they were intended to be users only. These include the Terminal IMPs then on the network (AMES, MITRE, RADC, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, NOAA, SAAC, ARPA and BBN) and the Network Control Center computer (address 5), which only gathers statistics. Also listed are Rand (7), Harvard (73), Lincoln (138), Illinois (12), NBS (19) and USC (23). The BBN Terminal IMP (address 158) is a prototype that is often disconnected while its programs are refined and debugged.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a two-week report on which network computers were up, plus a note that new software for the network's message handlers came out.

sections.title: The Host Status Table
sections.content: A table lists each host by network address, site and computer, with its status or prediction and who supplied it. Entries include Server, User Only, Never for the Network Control Center computer, a quoted "Soon", or a month. A star marks hosts not included in daily testing. The UCLA IBM-360/91 is listed as NETRJS now, with Telnet in June, and the table notes that the NMC (address 1) is a research site that would like prior arrangement with each user.
sections.plainLanguage: One list says what each computer does: serves others, only visits, or will be ready soon.

sections.title: The Daily Test Results
sections.content:
A second table gives results for each host on dates from 7/17 to 7/28, with the Eastern time of each test. Each cell is a code from the legend. A host counted as timed out (T) if it did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds.

The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered only a Network Job Service (NETRJS), which the Terminal IMP could not test, so a successful initial connection to the NETRJS logger was assumed to mean NETRJS was working. A hash mark before a result means the site advertised that its system might not be available at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each day a letter shows what happened when someone knocked on that computer's door.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

items.label: Full
items.desc: Host opened a connection, said all Network ports were in use, and closed it.

items.label: 1/2 Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection, then closed it or stopped responding.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: Host did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds.
